title: Connected components of hammocks give ordinary localization
statement:
Let $C$ be a small category and $W$ a wide subcategory. Use the reduced-hammock simplicial category $H(C,W)$ of [lem-coef-hammock-graph-colimit-presentation]. Let $C[W^{-1}]$ be the category with the same objects obtained by adjoining formal inverses to every arrow of $W$, subject to composition and inverse relations. Multiplying any row of a hammock in this ordinary localization, inverting the leftward arrows, induces a bijection
$$\pi_0 H(C,W)(x,y)\ \cong\ C[W^{-1}](x,y)$$
for all $x,y$. These bijections preserve identities and composition and are natural under functors of pairs. No freeness, calculus of fractions, or model-category structure is assumed.

source.place: Dwyer–Kan, Calculating simplicial localizations, Proposition 3.1, printed p.20. No Stacks tag states this result.

proof.text: Work with the explicit reduced diagrams of [lem-coef-hammock-graph-colimit-presentation]. For a simplicial set, use $\pi_0$ as vertices modulo the equivalence relation generated by the two endpoints of each 1-simplex. Thus here a component is represented by a reduced zigzag row, and a two-row hammock identifies its reduced rows. Concatenation descends to components: if two rows are the faces of a hammock, concatenate a fixed row on either side, repeated in both rows with identity vertical arrows. The result is an unreduced two-row hammock, and reduction gives an edge between the two concatenations. Apply this to every edge in a finite edge chain and to each factor in turn. Associativity follows because either parenthesization reduces the same concatenated list of columns; reduction has its specified well-defined value. The empty row is a unit. We obtain a category $B$ with the objects of $C$ and $B(x,y)=\pi_0 H(C,W)(x,y)$.

source.place: Definition 2.1, printed p.19; explicit component category construction

proof.text: Let $L=C[W^{-1}]$ with precisely the formal-arrow presentation in the statement. For a hammock with top vertices $A_i$, bottom vertices $B_i$, and downward vertical maps $v_i:A_i\to B_i$, let $r_i^A,r_i^B$ be its horizontal arrows read left to right in $L$ (invert each leftward arrow). A rightward square says $r_i^B v_{i-1}=v_i r_i^A$. For a leftward square with arrows $a_i:A_i\to A_{i-1}$ and $b_i:B_i\to B_{i-1}$, it says $b_i v_i=v_{i-1}a_i$; multiplying by the two inverses gives the same formula $b_i^{-1}v_{i-1}=v_i a_i^{-1}$. Hence multiplication across all columns gives $(r_l^B\cdots r_1^B)v_0=v_l(r_l^A\cdots r_1^A)$. Endpoint vertical maps are identities, so the two row products coincide. The same calculation applies to every adjacent pair in any width. Deleting identity columns and composing same-sign columns preserve the product by units and composition (for negative columns use $(ba)^{-1}=a^{-1}b^{-1}$). Consequently row product defines $F:B\to L$, preserving concatenation and empty rows.

source.place: Definitions 2.1 and 5.1, printed pp.19,24; Proposition 3.1, printed p.20; row-product square calculation

proof.text: Send $f:a\to b$ in $C$ to the component $j(f)$ of its one-column rightward row. Deleting an identity column gives $j(1_a)=1_a$ and composing two rightward columns gives $j(gf)=j(g)j(f)$. For $w:a\to b$ in $W$, let $k(w):b\to a$ be the component of its one-column leftward row. Here are both inverse identities, including their actual edges. In the shape $(+,-)$ with endpoints $a,a$, take top row $a\xrightarrow{1}a\xleftarrow{1}a$ and bottom row $a\xrightarrow{w}b\xleftarrow{w}a$, with middle downward map $w$ and endpoint downward identities. Both squares commute. In the shape $(-,+)$ with endpoints $b,b$, take top row $b\xleftarrow{w}a\xrightarrow{w}b$ and bottom row $b\xleftarrow{1}b\xrightarrow{1}b$, again with middle downward map $w$ and endpoint identities. Both squares commute. These are permitted unreduced hammocks: every negative and vertical arrow lies in $W$. Reducing each gives an edge from an identity component to a cancellation loop, or conversely. Thus $k(w)j(w)=1_a$ and $j(w)k(w)=1_b$, including when $w$ is an identity.

source.place: Definition 2.1 and Proposition 3.1, printed pp.19–20; explicit cancellation hammocks

proof.text: Define $J:L\to B$ on a formal composable word by replacing an ordinary arrow $f$ with $j(f)$ and an inverse letter $w^{-1}$ with $k(w)$, and composing in $B$. This descends through every defining relation of $L$: identity and ordinary composition are respected by $j$, and the two inverse relations were checked in Step 3. Relations in a longer word are respected by composing with its prefix and suffix; a finite chain of relation replacements therefore has the same image. Empty words and concatenation show that $J$ is a functor. Now $FJ$ fixes ordinary arrows and inverse letters and hence every finite word, so $FJ=1_L$. Every vertex of $H(C,W)(x,y)$ is a finite reduced row. Applying $JF$ to its component replaces each horizontal arrow with the component of that same one-column row and concatenates them; reduction recovers the original row. Hence $JF=1_B$ on every component. This proves the required bijections; Step 2 shows they preserve identities and composition.

source.place: Proposition 3.1, printed p.20; finite-word construction of the inverse and both inverse checks

proof.text: For a functor of pairs $T:(C,W)\to(C\prime,W\prime)$, the graph-presentation naturality clause applies entrywise to every raw hammock, followed by reduction. The induced ordinary-localization functor sends $f$ to $T(f)$ and the formal inverse $w^{-1}$ to $T(w)^{-1}$; it respects all word relations since $T$ preserves identities, compositions and $W$. The product of any image row is consequently the image of its product. If $T$ turns additional arrows into identities or identifies objects, subsequent reduction still preserves this product by Step 2. Thus the row-product bijections commute with both induced functors on every component, proving naturality without any chosen-generator or faithfulness assumption.

source.place: Section 3.4, printed p.21; Proposition 3.1, printed p.20; entrywise naturality
